name: Fermentation Lab
author: @praisejamesx
tagline: Track the batch, not just the bubble.
summary: A batch log for home fermentation that reads the live array as a change detector, compares its phase estimate to the logged pH, gravity, and temperature, and keeps every safety verdict on the primary controls.
scope: Support one batch at a time: log pH, temperature, gravity, and visible faults; state the recipe boundary; and surface where a same-array change signal disagrees with those primary controls. It does not certify safety and does not identify a pathogen or a toxin.
limits: Not a pathogen or toxin test. pH, time, temperature, recipe, and visible evidence decide; a pleasant smell cannot clear a batch.
Not a pH meter and not a concentration measurement. The array sees a cross-sensitive mixture.
Same array, same sample preparation, same distance. The array panel does not transfer across rigs.
A sealed ferment displaces oxygen with CO₂, which can flatten a MOX response without the fermentation stopping.
The array phase is a shape estimate from one window, not a laboratory measurement of fermentation stage.
whatItIs: A protocol, log, and decision-support workspace for home fermentation. It helps you record what changed, compare a batch to a reference blank on the same array, and stop when the primary controls say stop.
whatItIsNot: Not a pathogen test, not a pH meter, not a universal fermentation classifier, and not a cross-rig claim. A pleasant smell cannot clear a batch.

home.headline: The batch is the record, not the bubble.
home.detail: pH, temperature, gravity, recipe, and visible faults decide. The array adds a same-array phase estimate and names where it disagrees with those controls.

widgets.title: Fermentation Lab
widgets.subtitle: A batch log that keeps the sensor honest.
widgets.note: Example Vial · sandboxed cockpit · host-owned data

widgets.headline: Food safety is not a smell test.
widgets.body: A Vial can tell you a sample changed on your array. It cannot tell you a batch is safe. pH, time, temperature, recipe, and visible evidence decide.
always: Use a calibrated pH meter and a tested recipe.
Log every batch: date, salt or brine, temperature, pH, gravity, and visual cues.
When in doubt, discard. Discard is a valid batch outcome.
never: Never use a pleasant smell to overrule mould, slime, or a pH above 4.6 in a low-acid ferment.
Never sell or serve a batch you cannot trace.
Never compare readings from a different array or rig.

widgets.title: What this workspace is allowed to claim

items.label: Array can do
items.hint: Lag, active, stationary, or decline beyond the array's own noise on one window.

items.label: Array cannot do
items.hint: No pathogen, toxin, or “safe to eat” call. Ever.

items.label: Primary controls
items.hint: These decide. The nose only flags where something changed or disagrees.

widgets.title: The vessel, as a checklist
widgets.caption: Click a point. Every point is a place where a clean batch can turn into a risk.

hotspots.label: Airlock
hotspots.body: Gas should escape, not pressurise. Check the seal and keep the airlock clean. A dry airlock is not proof of safety.

hotspots.label: Lid / seal
hotspots.body: A sealed anaerobic vessel is exactly why low-acid ferments need a proven recipe and pH control. Do not improvise a low-acid anaerobic batch.

hotspots.label: Brine line
hotspots.body: Keep solids submerged. A surface exposed to air is a mould opportunity, not a flavour choice.

hotspots.label: Active ferment
hotspots.body: Bubbles and cloudiness are process cues. They are not a safety certificate. Log them with pH and temperature.

hotspots.label: Sensor port
hotspots.body: Use the array as a change detector against a clean reference on the same channels. Ethanol and acids can dominate the response; high VOC can saturate or poison MOX sensors.

steps.label: Prep
steps.body: Clean the vessel and hands. Weigh salt or measure brine. Label the batch. Record starting pH, gravity, and temperature.

steps.label: Lag
steps.body: Bubbles may be quiet and the array may not move beyond noise. Keep solids submerged. Log pH, temperature, gravity, smell, and anything visible.
steps.warn: No array movement and no acidity at day 3 is a prompt to verify the seal, temperature, and pH — not to assume it is safe.

steps.label: Active
steps.body: Acidity should move toward the recipe target and gravity should fall. Keep temperature stable. Off-odours, slime, or fuzzy growth are stop signals.

steps.label: Finish
steps.body: Chill or package exactly as the tested recipe says. Keep the batch record. Smell never overrides the recipe.

widgets.title: Batch log
widgets.description: The log is the valuable object. The sensor reading is one column, not the verdict.

widgets.title: pH trajectory
widgets.note: The line is your log, labeled EXAMPLE until you have two readings. It is not a target and not a safety curve. Follow the recipe and measure pH.

rules.when: pH above 4.6 after 48 h in a low-acid ferment
rules.then: Stop. Chill or discard per the recipe; verify with a calibrated meter. Do not rely on smell.

rules.when: Fuzzy, pink, black, or blue mould
rules.then: Discard. Do not salvage by removing the surface. Toxins can be invisible.

rules.when: Slime, rope, or a foul turn in the smell
No bubbles, no acidity, warm room, day 3
rules.then: Treat as stalled or risky. Verify pH and temperature; do not assume it is safe.

rules.when: Clean sour smell, pH in target, no visible faults
rules.then: Continue the protocol. This is not a safety certificate.

items.label: Vessel and hands clean
items.detail: No residue, no cracks, no exposed surfaces.

items.label: pH meter calibrated
items.detail: A reading you do not trust is worse than no reading.

items.label: Salt or brine measured by weight
items.detail: Volume spoons drift; weight is reproducible.

items.label: Temperature logged
items.detail: Warm is faster, not automatically safer.

items.label: Discard rule understood
items.detail: Decide now, not when the batch is emotionally valuable.

widgets.title: Use this with your rig
widgets.body: Record a clean reference blank, then a batch sample on the same channels and sample prep. Compare with Check. If the arrays differ, the app will refuse the comparison. The array panel is optional context; the batch log works without it.

docs.title: How to use this workspace
body: Start one batch. Fill the batch fields, then add a reading whenever you measure pH, temperature, or gravity, or inspect the vessel.
The verdict uses the structured visible-fault choice, pH, temperature, ferment type, and target. Free-text smell and visual notes are context; they are not keyword triggers.

The array panel reads the host's baseline-relative response and states where its phase estimate disagrees with the log. The Vial profile is the change detector: the host requires at least two corroborating channels and applies the profile's persistence, hysteresis, confidence floor, and coverage gate.
The stop rules are deliberately conservative. A sensor reading cannot clear a batch; it can only add a prompt to look, measure, or discard.

docs.title: What the sensor is actually doing
body: A MOX array responds to a mixture of volatile compounds. Ethanol, organic acids, and other fermentation products can dominate the response, and high concentrations can saturate or poison a sensor.
The useful signal is a change relative to a reference on the same array. The absolute number is not concentration and is not comparable across rigs.

Metal-oxide sensors respond to humidity and temperature as well as to reducing gases. The array phase is withheld when the vessel environment moves more than two degrees or eight percent relative humidity during the window.
A sealed ferment displaces oxygen with CO₂. That can flatten or shift the response without the fermentation stopping, which is why a flat array is never read as “finished”.

docs.title: How the array phase is estimated
body: The workspace takes the median baseline-relative response across live, non-dead channels, over roughly the last three minutes of the host window.

It compares the change across that window to the median two-times-CV noise band of the same channels. A change inside the band is not movement. The band explains the phase; it is not the profile detector.

The profile detector is the authoritative change call. The host requires at least two channels to clear their sensitivity-scaled budget, applies the 120 s warning persistence with 30% hysteresis, the 0.6 confidence floor, and the 80% coverage gate. A phase that moves without profile confirmation is shown as a shape estimate, not a confirmed change.

The estimate has four states: lag (near the baseline and flat), active (rising beyond noise), stationary (elevated but flat), and decline (falling beyond noise). An active phase that has lost more than half its rate is labeled slowing.
A new phase must hold for three consecutive windows before it is written to the journal, and at most once a minute. A phase that flickers with noise is not an observation.
The estimate is descriptive. It is not a lab measurement, not a completion test, and it never overrules pH, gravity, temperature, or a visible fault.

docs.title: What the disagreement notes mean
body: Acidity still falling while the array is flat: CO₂ displacement or sensor behaviour can flatten the array. Keep measuring pH; do not read the flat trace as finished.
Array rising while pH is flat: one of the two signals is misleading. Verify the pH meter calibration and add a reading before drawing a conclusion.
No array movement by day three: slow start, cold vessel, poor seal, or a sensor that is not seeing the headspace. Verify the seal and temperature, then re-check pH.
Gravity flat while the array moves: re-measure gravity and inspect the vessel. The two signals should be reconciled before packaging.
Every note is a prompt to check a primary control. It is not a diagnosis and it is not a safety verdict.

docs.title: What can go wrong
body: Low-acid, anaerobic ferments can support Clostridium botulinum growth. Smell is not a reliable botulinum test. Follow a tested recipe, use a calibrated pH meter, and respect the pH 4.6 boundary for low-acid foods.
Moulds can produce mycotoxins that are not removed by scraping the surface. Discard fuzzy or coloured growth.
Cross-contamination from hands, utensils, or an airlock turns a clean batch into an uncontrolled one.
A drifted or saturated sensor can make a changing batch look stable. The log and the primary measurements matter more than the trace.

docs.title: How to validate a Vial on your rig
body: Record a clean reference blank and at least three batch samples on the same array, with the same sample preparation and distance.
Use Check to compare the reference and the batch. Read the lower bound and the permutation p-value, not just the badge.
A sealed Vial is a claim about a closed-set comparison on the array that produced the evidence. It is not a transferable calibration and it is not a safety certification.

docs.title: The profile is a starting point, not evidence
body: The declared profile uses a 300 s warmup, a 120 s R0 window, a three-sample median, delta-over-R0 response, a two-channel corroboration floor, and a 120 s warning persistence with 30% hysteresis.

The host now enforces the corroboration floor, the confidence floor, and the coverage gate on the live path. Those are contract behaviour, not measured performance. The defaults have not been measured against a held-out fermentation dataset, so the Vial installs as Ungated.
Add a held-out report to the evidence block before describing any of these values as validated.

docs.title: Cleaning and traceability
body: Clean the vessel, lid, airlock, weights, and hands before the batch. Keep raw and finished batches separate.
Label every batch with date, recipe, salt or brine, and starting temperature. A batch you cannot trace is a batch you cannot debug.
